extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent examiners and patent applicants/prosecutors (practitioners interacting with CIPO)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on Canadian patent-office procedural standards for deposits of biological material, filing protests/prior art, notices of allowance/conditional allowance, amendments, withdrawals, Final Actions (rejections) and the content/structure of Final Action reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of deposited biological material (Rule 11.3(a) / subsection 97(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: After a request form for the furnishing of a sample of deposited biological material has been filed with the Commissioner of Patents, the Commissioner will, in accordance with subsection 97(2) of the Patent Rules, make the certification referred to in Rule 11.3(a) of the Regulations Under the Budapest Treaty that the deposit is referred to in an application for patent in Canada, that the requester has fulfilled all conditions for the furnishing of a sample, and that the requester has a right to a sample of the deposited material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copy of the request along with the certification is sent to the requester in accordance with subsection 97(3) of the Patent Rules or, where the requester is an independent expert, to the applicant and to the person who requested the nomination of the expert in accordance with subsection 98(2) of the Patent Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to obtain a sample from a pending application (no restriction under subsection 95(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps to obtain a sample of biological material referred to in a pending Canadian patent application on which no restriction has been placed under subsection 95(1) of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requesting party completes parts I–IV of the request form; prepares a letter of undertaking agreeing to abide by conditions in paragraph 97(2)(b); under a covering letter sends the letter and request form to the Commissioner per MOPOP 2.02 correspondence procedures; the Commissioner or designate completes part V, certifies with the Patent Office seal and returns it under covering letter; the requesting party sends the request form, a purchase order and any fee to the IDA; the IDA sends a sample of the biological material to the requesting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to obtain a sample via an independent expert (restriction under subsection 95(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps to release a sample of a biological material referred to in a pending Canadian application, on which a restriction has been placed under subsection 95(1), to an independent expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesting party asks Commissioner to nominate an independent expert; Commissioner (with applicant agreement) nominates the expert; the independent expert completes parts I–IV of the request form and prepares a letter of undertaking per paragraph 97(2)(b); under a covering letter the expert sends the letter and request form to the Commissioner per MOPOP 2.02; Commissioner completes part V, certifies with the Patent Office seal and sends the completed request form to the requesting party and a copy to the applicant; the requesting party sends the request form, purchase order and fee to the IDA; the IDA sends the sample to the independent expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to obtain a sample from an issued, refused, withdrawn or abandoned patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps to obtain a sample of a biological material referred to in an issued patent, or a patent application that has been refused, withdrawn or deemed abandoned and beyond the period of reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requesting party writes to the IDA with a purchase order giving name and address and accession number; include evidence that the patent has been issued or that the application has been refused/withdrawn/abandoned (e.g., cover page of Canadian patent or Canadian Patent Database status); submit fee where required; if IDA requires certification, requester sends the request form to the Commissioner per MOPOP 2.02; Commissioner completes part V, certifies with seal and returns it; requester sends request form to IDA; IDA sends sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing prior art under section 34.1 — permitted content and formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may file prior art with the Commissioner consisting of patents, applications for patents open to public inspection and printed publications that the person believes have a bearing on the patentability of any claim in a patent application. Prior art filed under section 34.1 must be accompanied by an explanation of why the art is pertinent and must follow the general written communications requirements of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions will be acknowledged but the provider will not be directly informed regarding any resulting action. The examiner will not discuss prosecution with the provider; the provider may access the prosecution file when opened to public inspection. Prior art is made part of the application file and the applicant is notified. If the referred application is a PCT not yet in national phase, the Office retains the submission until the late national entry date has passed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protests — submission requirements and identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Any written communication submitted to the Commissioner before grant with the stated or apparent intention of protesting the granting of a patent must follow general written communications requirements and will be acknowledged; the protestor will not be directly informed regarding any resulting action but has access to the prosecution file when opened to public inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protestor should identify the Canadian patent application number, or at least the inventor or applicant, to allow identification. Failure to identify an application by number, inventor or applicant reduces the likelihood of locating the application and reduces the effectiveness of the protest. When a protest does not identify an application, the Patent Office will search to identify it; if found, the protest is made part of the file and the applicant is notified. If a specific application cannot be located, the Office will retain the protest for two years while attempting to identify the relevant application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of protests and filings of prior art by the examiner — timing and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A protest or filing of prior art is only considered by the patent examiner after examination of the application has been requested. Information is taken into account by the examiner if found pertinent and will be used during prosecution accordingly; pertinence may determine whether a notice of allowance will be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the protest or prior art calls the patentability of the application into question, the Notice of Allowance will be withdrawn and the application returned to the examiner for further consideration. Protests may contain affidavits; affidavits should support allegations with dated material or give details to locate such material. Affidavits with allegations unsupported by dated documentation will usually be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality limits for protests and prior art filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Any protest or filing of prior art will become part of the laid-open application file and will be made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party requests confidentiality for a protest or filing, the material will be returned to the sender and will not be considered by the examiner. Parties cannot remain anonymous; identifying information (e.g., as provided in the cover letter) will be made public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of allowance — issuance and final fee deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner has reasonable grounds to believe a patent application complies with the Patent Act and Patent Rules, the Commissioner will notify the applicant via a notice of allowance and require payment of the final fee no later than four months after the date of the notice; failure to pay within that period results in deemed abandonment under paragraph 132(1)(f) of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final fee includes a basic fee, a fee per page of specification/drawings in excess of 100 (excluding electronic sequence listing pages), and an excess claim fee for each claim in excess of 20 not already paid when requesting examination. See CIPO Patent Fees for amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final fee composition and excess claim fee calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The final fee is composed of the basic fee, a fee for each page of the specification and drawings in excess of 100 (other than pages of a sequence listing submitted electronically), and an excess claim fee for each claim in excess of 20 that was not already paid when requesting examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To calculate the excess claim fee, the Office looks at the maximum number of excess claims in the application from the date of the request for examination until the application is allowed. Example: if requested with 26 claims (6 excess), amendments raise to 30 (10 excess), later to 18 (maximum unchanged), the maximum during the period is 30 so excess claim fees are charged for 10 excess claims; if 6 were already paid, the notice requires payment for 4 additional excess claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional notice of allowance — scope, examples of minor defects, and reply consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an examiner believes the application contains only certain minor defects which, if corrected, would allow the application, the Commissioner will issue a conditional notice of allowance indicating the outstanding minor defects and requiring satisfactory amendments or arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of minor defects include failing to meet margin requirements; failing to meet line spacing or font size; failure to have petition/abstract/description/claims each begin on a new page; failure to consecutively number pages; inclusion of drawings in petition/abstract/description/claims; trademarks included without identification; incorporation of documents by reference; references to documents not available to the public; failure to comply with sequence listing requirements; failure to comply with drawing requirements. The notice requires amendments to address defects and payment of the final fee within four months. If the applicant does not reply in good faith and the final fee is not paid, the application is deemed abandoned under paragraph 132(1)(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments after notice of allowance or conditional notice — permitted amendments and consequences of impermissible amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination ceases once a notice of allowance has been sent; amendments after a notice of allowance are not permitted unless the notice is withdrawn or the amendment corrects an obvious error. After a conditional notice of allowance, amendments are limited to those that address the defects identified or correct obvious errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an impermissible amendment is submitted after a conditional notice of allowance, the notice will be withdrawn and the application will be examined without taking into account the impermissible amendments and any other amendments made from the day the conditional notice was sent until the day it was withdrawn (subsection 100(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of obvious errors after notice/conditional notice — criteria and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may amend obvious errors in the specification and drawings after a notice of allowance if the amendment is submitted on or before the date of payment of the final fee; after a conditional notice if submitted on or before the date on which the applicant replies in good faith to the conditional notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basis for obviousness is the specifications and drawings contained in the application on the day the notice or conditional notice was sent. An amendment is permissible if it is obvious that something other than what appears was intended and that nothing other than the proposed amendment could have been intended; the examiner makes the final determination. There is no fee for the correction. The mechanism does not include replacement of pages for 'better quality' (identical pages replacing inferior quality are considered amendments and not acceptable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of notice of allowance or conditional notice — grounds and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner will withdraw a notice of allowance before a patent is issued if the examiner has reasonable grounds to believe the application does not comply with the Patent Act and Patent Rules, except when the defects would not affect the readability, clarity or validity of the patent if granted; the notice will not be withdrawn if the application is deemed abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application may be withdrawn from allowance in view of applicable prior art identified in a protest or filing of prior art. The Commissioner will inform the applicant by notice that the notice of allowance has been withdrawn and refund the final fee if paid. A conditional notice can be withdrawn where the applicant's reply (made in good faith) is later assessed as non-compliant because defects remain or the reply introduces impermissible amendments; if withdrawn, any amendments made after the conditional notice and before withdrawal are considered never to have been made, and the applicant will be informed of outstanding defects in an examiner's report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance of a patent on payment of final fee — processing order and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the applicant pays the final fee and, if applicable, corrects any minor defects noted in a conditional notice of allowance, the Office will prepare the application to issue a granted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the payment is conditional (e.g., upon recordal of a transfer under section 49 or upon amendment of an obvious error), the Office will process those requests before starting preparations to grant the patent so the currently recognized applicant or patentee will always be listed. Consult CIPO's service standards for expected time to prepare a granted patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a Final Action (rejection) is warranted — decision factors
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may reject an application where subsection 86(3) is met: the examiner previously identified a defect and requisitioned the applicant; the applicant replied; but the examiner believes the application still does not comply with the Act or Rules in respect of one or more defects and that the applicant will not amend to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to reject must consider overall context: length of prior prosecution, the nature of outstanding defects, the extent to which these were discussed, and the likelihood that further prosecution would lead to allowance. Broadly, a Final Action is desirable when all defects are resolved other than the impasse, but may be issued earlier to avoid unduly prolonging prosecution. New defects introduced late by the applicant require examiner judgment whether to delay rejection for further report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-final action practice and warning before Final Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it appears prosecution is approaching an impasse, an examiner will usually advise the applicant in the report that a further report on substantially the same points may be made final; the last report before a Final Action (a 'pre-final' action) should provide fully elaborated arguments supporting the examiner's conclusion that the application is defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the applicant's opportunities to amend post-rejection may be limited, it is important to ensure all defects have been identified in a pre-final action. Advising the applicant that the examiner is considering making the next report a Final Action helps the applicant take special care in responding to the pre-final action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and structure requirements for a Final Action report
rubrics_metrics.description: A Final Action is a particular type of examiner's report containing a requisition under subsection 86(5), prominently labelled FINAL ACTION (or 'Décision finale'), and indicating rejection under subsection 86(3) (or subsection 199(1) where applicable). The preamble should identify in broad terms the defects leading to rejection and which claims are defective or allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report should be drafted to make the point of disagreement clear, set out the applicant's position as understood by the examiner, and the examiner's reasoning for concluding the application does not comply despite applicant arguments. Where relevant, the report should include: a summary of the application emphasizing relevant claims; identification of any allowable claims; identification and discussion of relevant prior art; summary of relevant prior prosecution; discussion of legal/jurisprudential/administrative considerations central to the dispute; comprehensive grounds for rejection including rebuttal of applicant's arguments; and a brief summation recapitulating grounds for rejection. It may be beneficial to divide the report into sections with clear headings. To the extent practical, the Final Action should be understandable independently of other reports or responses so that interested persons (applicant, Patent Appeal Board, Commissioner, Court) can readily understand the dispute and reasoning.
